questions.q: The opening script did Number(env.PORT ?? "3000") with PORT=80x. Why is this worse than it looks?
questions.explain: Number("80x") is NaN, not an error. The config loader parses with a pattern and reports PORT must be a whole number… before anything connects.
options: It produces NaN silently, and the failure shows up later, far from the typo, after connections are already open

questions.q: Why does loadConfig collect every problem instead of throwing at the first one?
questions.explain: Every failed deploy costs time. Reporting all problems at once turns three round trips into one. The app still does not start: the error is thrown after the loop.
options: A deploy with three bad settings should fail once with three messages, not three times with one each
TypeScript does not allow throwing inside a loop
So the app can start with partial configuration

questions.q: What does ConfigOf<typeof schema> give you?
questions.explain: It is a mapped type: each key of the schema becomes a readonly property of the type inside its Setting. The runtime check is loadConfig; the type follows from the same object.
options: A runtime check of the environment
The config's TypeScript type, computed from the schema, so the two cannot drift apart
A copy of the schema with defaults filled in
A list of the environment variable names

questions.q: loadConfig(schema, envFile, processEnv): the .env file says LOG_LEVEL=debug, the real environment says LOG_LEVEL=warn. What is the result, and why is that order right?
questions.explain: Defaults, then files, then the environment: each layer is more specific to where the process runs. An operator must be able to change a setting without editing files in the image.
options: warn: later layers win, and the real environment of a deployed process must be able to override a developer's file
An error, because the two sources disagree

questions.q: Why log safeView(schema, config) instead of config?
questions.explain: Logs are copied, shipped, searched and kept for months by many people and systems. A secret that reaches them is effectively leaked.
options: Secret settings (database URL with a password, session secret) are replaced, so they never reach the log store

questions.q: Why does the container dispose instances in reverse creation order?
questions.explain: Dependencies are always created before their dependents, so reverse creation order closes dependents first. Closing the pool first would break the repository's last operations.
options: Because arrays are faster to read backwards
An object created later may depend on one created earlier (a repository on a pool), so the dependent must be closed first
It does not matter; any order is fine

questions.q: The mini container does not track transient instances for disposal. Why?
questions.explain: A transient resolved a million times would mean a million references held forever: a memory leak. The garbage collector frees memory, but it never calls dispose, so a transient that holds a connection must be closed by its owner.
options: A transient belongs to whoever asked for it; tracking every one at the root would keep them all alive for the life of the process
Transients are disposed by the garbage collector automatically, including closing their connections

questions.q: A singleton ReportService depends on the scoped Cart. Why does the container refuse?
questions.explain: That is a captive dependency: a longer-lived object capturing a shorter-lived one. The container catches it at resolve time and names the chain.
options: The singleton would keep the first request's cart forever and show it to every later request
Scoped objects cannot be created from a factory
It would create a circular dependency

questions.q: What does logger.child({ requestId: "req-7" }) give you?
questions.explain: Bound fields save every call site from repeating them, and they cannot be forgotten. The framework creates one child per request and per module.
options: A logger with a lower level
A logger that adds requestId to every entry it writes, so one request's entries can be found together
A copy of the parent's entries
A logger that writes to a separate file

questions.q: The logger's sink throws "disk full". What should happen to the request that called logger.info?
questions.explain: Logging observes the work; it is not the work. A real logger also counts dropped entries so the outage is visible in metrics.
options: It should continue; a logging failure must not break the business operation
It should retry the log line until it succeeds

questions.q: Components start in the order database, queue, http, and http fails. What does the mini lifecycle do?
questions.explain: Rollback stops what already started, in reverse order, so nothing stays half-open, and the error tells you which component failed and why.
options: Leaves database and queue running and throws
Stops queue, then database, sets the state to failed, and throws a StartupError naming http with the original error as its cause

questions.q: On the same failure, @zudojs/lifecycle also calls stop on http, the component that failed. What does that ask of component authors?
questions.explain: Stopping a half-started component frees what it did manage to open (a bound port, a file). The price is that stop must be safe in any state.
options: Every stop must work even when its start did not finish, for example check whether the server is actually listening
Components must be registered in order

questions.q: Why wrap every start in a timeout?
questions.explain: A named timeout turns "the deploy is stuck" into "search-index start timed out after 5000 ms", and the rollback still runs.
options: A dependency that accepts a connection and never answers would otherwise leave the process starting forever, with no error that names it

questions.q: withTimeout calls clearTimeout in a finally block. What goes wrong without it?
questions.explain: An active timer keeps the event loop busy, so a process that should exit after stop hangs until every forgotten timer fires.
options: After a successful start, a pending timer keeps the Node process alive (and later rejects a promise nobody is waiting for)

questions.q: Two signals arrive at once and stop() is called twice. What does the mini lifecycle do?
questions.explain: Storing the in-progress promise makes stop idempotent. Stopping a database pool twice would throw or hang in many drivers.
options: The second call gets the same promise as the first, so each component stops once and both callers wait for the end

questions.q: During shutdown, the queue's stop throws. What should happen to the database's stop, which comes after it?
questions.explain: Leaving the database open because the queue misbehaved is worse than a noisy log. Shutdown is best-effort for every component.
options: It is skipped, because shutdown failed
It still runs; the queue's error is logged

questions.q: What is SIGTERM, and what does Node do with it when no handler is installed?
questions.explain: Kubernetes and systemd send SIGTERM, wait a grace period, then kill the process. The handler turns that window into a graceful stop.
options: A request to reload configuration; Node ignores it
The polite "please stop" an orchestrator sends before killing a process; without a handler Node exits at once, cutting off in-flight work
A crash report; Node prints a stack trace
A signal that only exists on Windows

questions.q: What happens if you register a service with @zudojs/container's registerFactory and no scope option?
questions.explain: The default is transient. A connection pool registered without a scope would be created again for every resolve; pass ContainerScope.SINGLETON for shared resources.
options: It is transient: a new instance on every resolve

questions.q: @zudojs/config's toSafeObject redacted database_url although it was never marked secret. Why?
questions.explain: Value-based detection catches secrets hidden in settings with harmless names. Your mini loader only knows what the schema marks secret.
options: It detects sensitive entries by key name and by value, and a URL with a password in it looks sensitive
It was marked secret by the environment source

questions.q: With @zudojs/logger, logger.error("payment failed", { cause: new Error("card declined") }) logged "cause":{}. Why?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify(new Error("x")) is {}. Your mini logger converted Error fields to name and message; with the package, log the message explicitly.
options: An error's message and stack are not enumerable properties, so serialising the nested object finds nothing

questions.q: Write a tiny container with register(token, factory) (singletons only) and resolve(token). resolve must throw nothing registered for <name> for an unknown token. The program should print same: true and nothing registered for Mailer.
questions.explain: The token object is the key and carries the type, so resolve(POOL) is typed without a cast at the call site. The one cast lives inside the container, where the invariant "stored under a Token<T>, so it is a T" holds.
questions.expected:
same: true
nothing registered for Mailer

questions.q: Write loadPort(env): it returns 3000 when PORT is missing, the number when PORT is 1 to 65535 digits-only, and otherwise throws PORT must be a whole number from 1 to 65535, got "<value>". The program should print 3000, 8080, and the error for "80x".
questions.explain: Checking the text with a pattern before converting catches "80x", "8.5" and " ", which Number would turn into NaN, 8.5 and 0. The error names the variable and the bad value.
questions.expected:
3000
8080
PORT must be a whole number from 1 to 65535, got "80x"

questions.q: Write createLogger(level, fields = {}) returning { info, warn, child }. It prints one JSON line per entry, {"level":…,"message":…, …fields}, drops entries below the level (info < warn), and child(extra) adds fields. The program should print exactly the two lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: The child keeps the parent's level and fields and adds its own, so every entry of the request carries requestId. Filtering happens before any string is built, which keeps disabled debug logging cheap.

questions.q: Write startAll(parts): start each part in order; if one throws, stop the started ones in reverse and rethrow. The program should print the lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: metrics never starts, http failed, and the two that started are stopped newest first. Rethrowing keeps the original error for the caller.
questions.expected:
start database
start queue
stop queue
stop database
http failed

questions.q: Write createScope() that returns { resolveCart(), dispose() }: resolveCart returns the same cart within one scope, and dispose calls the cart's dispose once if one was created. The program should print the three lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: Each scope caches its own cart, so one request's items never reach another. Disposing a scope that never created a cart does nothing: disposal only closes what was actually created.
questions.expected:
separate carts: true
released cart with 2 items
done

questions.q: Write levels(deps): group the names so that each group depends only on earlier groups. Each name's level is 0 without dependencies, otherwise one more than its highest dependency. The program should print [ [ 'database', 'cache' ], [ 'catalog', 'orders' ], [ 'http' ] ].
questions.explain: Everything in one group can start at the same time with Promise.all; the groups run one after another. The stable sort keeps names of the same level in their original order.

questions.q: This file is an ES module, so it runs in strict mode. What does this print?
questions.explain: In strict mode, writing to a frozen object's property throws a TypeError; in sloppy scripts it would fail silently. Either way the value stays 8080. The cast only silenced the compiler, which would otherwise refuse the write because of readonly.

questions.q: Write withTimeout(work, ms, what): resolve with the work's result, or reject with <what> timed out after <ms> ms if it takes longer, and always clear the timer. The program should print ready and queue start timed out after 30 ms.
questions.explain: Promise.race settles with whichever promise settles first. The timeout does not cancel the slow work; it only stops waiting for it, which is why a lifecycle rolls back after a timeout.
questions.expected:
ready
queue start timed out after 30 ms

questions.q: Write stopAll(parts): stop the parts in the given order; when one throws, record "<name>: <message>" in a list and continue. Return the list of failures. The program should print the lines shown in the expected output.
questions.explain: Shutdown is best effort: one component's failure is reported, and the database still closes. Returning the failures lets the caller log them and choose a non-zero exit code.

http stopped
database stopped
[ 'queue: broker unreachable' ]
